questions.question: Define sustainable development and explain, using externalities, public goods and the tragedy of the commons, why a free market systematically damages the environment.
questions.expected_answer: Sustainable development, from the Brundtland Commission of 1987, is development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, resting on economic, social and environmental legs — with natural resources treated as capital, so growth that consumes them is spending inheritance, not earning income. The market fails the environment in three ways. Externalities: a polluting factory imposes real costs — dead fish, illness, treatment — on people outside its transactions, so its private cost sits below the true social cost, its output is priced too cheaply, and too much is produced; pollution is what the price system delivers when part of the cost is invisible. Public goods: clean air and a stable climate are non-excludable and non-rival, so no one can charge for them, no private firm supplies them, and everyone free-rides on others' restraint. Missing property rights: the tragedy of the commons — an ownerless fish stock, forest or atmosphere is raced to exhaustion because each user correctly reasons that what they spare, another will take; what everybody owns, nobody protects. The policy logic follows directly: make invisible costs visible, price the unpriced, and give the ownerless an owner or a rule.

questions.question: Compare command-and-control measures with market-based measures for ensuring sustainability, giving South African examples of each and stating when each is appropriate.
questions.expected_answer: Command and control regulates directly: emission standards, zoning, environmental impact assessments, protected areas, and quotas or licences for fishing and water use. Its strengths are certainty and enforceability where danger is acute; its weaknesses are costly inspection, no reward for beating the minimum, and uniform rules that ignore differing clean-up costs across firms. Market-based measures price the externality so the polluter pays: South Africa's carbon tax, in force since 2019 as Africa's first, prices each ton of carbon dioxide, while the plastic-bag and tyre levies apply the same logic at the till — a tax makes the social cost private and polices itself, since every unit not polluted is money saved. Subsidies pull where taxes push: solar water heater rebates and the renewable procurement programme that built wind and solar capacity. Tradable permits cap total pollution and let firms trade allowances — the cap fixes the environmental outcome while trading finds the cheapest cutters, as in the EU emissions trading scheme; a tax fixes the price and discovers the quantity, permits fix the quantity and discover the price. Assigning property rights cures the commons where feasible — community conservancies make wildlife a defended village asset — and supporting measures include education, eco-labelling, green procurement and rehabilitation programmes like Working for Water. The mixing rule: standards where poison is acute, taxes for continuous efficient incentives, permits where a hard cap is the point.

questions.question: Trace the major international environmental agreements from Montreal to the recent COPs, contrasting the designs of Kyoto and Paris, and explain South Africa's Just Energy Transition Partnership.
questions.expected_answer: Montreal 1987 phased out ozone-destroying CFCs and succeeded completely — the healing ozone layer is the standing proof that global cooperation can work. Rio 1992, the Earth Summit, produced Agenda 21, the Convention on Biological Diversity and the UNFCCC, whose principle of common but differentiated responsibilities requires all to act but the carbon-built rich to carry more. Kyoto 1997 set binding quantified cuts for developed countries only; with the United States never ratifying and major emerging emitters outside the targets, its coverage shrank — teaching that binding-for-some cannot move a global curve. Johannesburg 2002 focused on implementation, linking environment to poverty, water and energy. Paris 2015 inverted the design: nearly universal membership through self-set, five-yearly, progressively tightened nationally determined contributions, aiming well below two degrees and pursuing 1,5 — universal where Kyoto was partial, voluntary where Kyoto was binding, its strength and weakness in one design, enforced by transparency, the ratchet and the global stocktake rather than courts. Recent COPs added Glasgow 2021's coal phase-down and carbon-market rules, Sharm el-Sheikh 2022's loss and damage fund for climate harm already unavoidable, and Dubai 2023's first global stocktake calling for transition away from fossil fuels. The Just Energy Transition Partnership, announced at Glasgow, pledges 8,5 billion dollars from wealthy nations to help coal-dependent South Africa decarbonise justly — retraining coal workers, bringing new industry to coal towns, and keeping electricity secure while the grid greens — carrying sustainability's social leg into energy policy.
